# How to Evaluate Patent AI Tools: A Pilot Checklist


February 17, 2026


[Caleb Harris](https://www.linkedin.com/in/caleb-m-harris/)


A patent AI tool can look excellent in a guided demo and still fail on a long dependent claim, scanned reference, or protected matter. A useful evaluation shows how the system handles your work, how much attorney review it requires, and whether its data practices fit your obligations. The right pilot gives decision-makers evidence they can use without flattening every concern into one number.


## Key takeaways


- Evaluate one defined workflow, with named users, inputs, work product, and a human baseline.
- Examine source fidelity, substantive completeness, corpus coverage, attorney control, security, workflow fit, adoption, support, and cost separately.
- Use representative work and known answers, including difficult and adversarial cases that expose patent-specific failure modes.
- Count review and correction time. Fast generation has little value if attorneys must rebuild the output.
- Treat confidentiality, access control, and fabricated sources as decision issues in their own right.


## 1. Define the job before comparing tools


“Patent AI” includes drafting assistants, prior art search systems, portfolio analytics platforms, and litigation workspaces. These products solve different jobs. A broad feature comparison tends to reward polished interfaces and long feature lists. A workflow test reveals whether a tool produces useful work.


Start with a one-page pilot brief:


- **Workflow:** Name one job, such as finding prior art for an invalidity theory, building an evidence-of-use chart, responding to an office action, or triaging a portfolio.
- **Users:** Identify the attorneys and staff who will perform and supervise the work after rollout.
- **Inputs:** List the patents, prosecution histories, non-patent literature (NPL), product manuals, videos, internal files, and other sources the job requires.
- **Work product:** Specify the expected deliverable and format, such as a reviewed claim chart in the firm’s Word template.
- **Baseline:** Document the current research, drafting, review, correction, administration, and outside spend.
- **Data class:** State whether the pilot will use public, sanitized, or separately approved information and what permissions apply.
- **Decision conditions:** Record the required capabilities, unacceptable failure modes, decision owner, and deadline before the vendor sees the test set.


For patent litigation teams, we recommend putting our AI workspace through this process first. We built it around prior art search, invalidity and infringement analysis, and source-linked claim charts with attorney-controlled exports. Prosecution drafting, docketing, and broad portfolio administration sit outside our core. Our guide to[patent litigation AI](https://www.tryandai.com/patent-litigation-ai) explains that category, and our comparison of[general and purpose-built AI](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/ai-for-patent-work-generic-vs-purpose-built) helps match the tool type to the job.


## 2. Examine each part of the working relationship


The evaluation should preserve meaningful differences between risks. Citation support, access controls, and user adoption answer different questions, so an aggregate rating can hide the reason a tool succeeds or fails.


Area to examine Questions the pilot should answer Evidence to keep


Accuracy and source fidelity Does every cited source exist, open at the stated location, and support the mapped limitation or assertion? Source-by-source review decisions and corrected examples


Substantive completeness Does the output address every required limitation, issue, field, instruction, and claim dependency? Missing, partial, and correctly handled units


Retrieval and corpus coverage Can the system search or ingest the patent, NPL, product, language, jurisdiction, and date sources the workflow needs? Known references found, accepted new material, and corpus gaps


Work-product quality Can attorneys edit and use the result in the required format without rebuilding its substance elsewhere? First-pass decisions, edits, and export samples


Attorney control and auditability Can reviewers inspect sources, reject or refine analysis, approve citations, preserve versions, and identify who took each action? Review history, permissions, versions, and audit exports


Security and confidentiality Do the contract and technical controls cover data use, retention, access, hosting, incidents, deletion, and subprocessors? Controlling terms, architecture answers, and control evidence


Workflow and administration Do identity, ingestion, matter access, templates, exports, and records fit the production environment? An end-to-end task and an administration log


Adoption, support, and reliability Can intended users finish the work, and does the vendor resolve substantive problems that recur? Completion records, help requests, reruns, and support tickets


Total cost and value Does the tool reduce the fully loaded cost or create useful capacity after review, training, integration, and administration? Time records, accepted outputs, invoices, and implementation estimates


Some findings should stop or narrow the pilot until they are resolved. Examples include an invented source, a decisive citation that does not support the mapping, client data use outside approved terms, access across a matter boundary, and an export path that bypasses required attorney approval. Formatting quality or a strong search result does not cure those problems.


## 3. Build a representative patent test set


A vendor-selected example proves that the tool can succeed once. Your test set should show whether it works repeatedly across the matters, technologies, documents, and jurisdictions your team handles.


Include ordinary work, difficult work, and adversarial cases designed to trigger a known failure. The set needs enough claim limitations, citations, known-reference opportunities, document types, and repeated runs to expose patterns. A small set with many substantive review decisions can be more useful than a large set of shallow prompts.


Use public, sanitized, or separately approved material. A matter’s closure does not make its files safe for a vendor pilot. The[former-client duty](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/professional_responsibility/publications/model_rules_of_professional_conduct/rule_1_9_duties_of_former_clients/comment_on_rule_1_9/) includes continuing confidentiality obligations.


Each test item should contain:


- **Frozen inputs:** The same claims, constructions, references, search dates, instructions, and file versions for every tool.
- **Expected result:** Accepted attorney work product, known relevant references, decisive passages, and any reasonable range of answers.
- **Named failure modes:** A definition of outcome-determinative, material, and minor problems for that task.
- **Human baseline:** Separate time for research, drafting, review, correction, and administration.
- **Review record:** A place to record each citation, limitation, omission, correction, and final acceptance decision.


Give vendors equivalent setup access and document any assistance they provide. Then run the test items without live steering. Record the product version, settings, prompts, source collection, run date, and run time. Qualified patent reviewers should inspect the substance. For high-stakes work, an independent second review and a documented resolution of disagreements reduce the chance that vendor preference drives the result.


## 4. Inspect accuracy at the source and claim-limitation level


Fluent prose is a poor proxy for patent accuracy. Patent work turns on whether a particular source discloses a particular limitation, whether the source qualifies for the asserted date, and whether the pinpoint passage supports the legal theory.


A[preregistered legal AI study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20362) found hallucinations in 17% to 33% of responses from three proprietary legal research systems. Those rates do not transfer to patent platforms, which the study did not test. The important lesson is narrower: a real-looking link can point to a source that fails to support the proposition.


The United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO)[AI guidance](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/04/11/2024-07629/guidance-on-use-of-artificial-intelligence-based-tools-in-practice-before-the-united-states-patent) states that reliance on an AI tool alone does not satisfy the reasonable-inquiry obligation. The person presenting a paper remains responsible for reviewing its contents and factual and legal support.


Keep these observations separate:


- **Citation existence:** Does the cited patent, publication, passage, figure, timestamp, or product document exist at the stated location?
- **Citation support:** Does that material disclose the mapped limitation or substantiate the assertion in context?
- **Limitation coverage:** Did the tool address every assigned limitation, including inherited elements in dependent claims?
- **Retrieval performance:** Did it return known relevant references early enough to review, and did it surface new references the reviewers accept?
- **First-pass usability:** Could an attorney refine the output, or did the substance and structure require reconstruction?
- **Repeatability:** Does the same configuration handle the hardest items consistently across repeated runs?
- **Review burden:** How much setup, monitoring, verification, correction, administration, and manual fallback did completion require?


Record the underlying counts and examples. A missing output still matters: its limitations, required issues, and time remain part of the evaluation record. Known-reference retrieval is a regression check rather than proof that the system found all relevant art. New accepted art is a gain, while a missed decisive reference remains a material finding.


For drafting, office-action response, evidence review, and portfolio triage, translate the same questions to the work. Check every source-bearing assertion, required section, instruction, input document, and classification decision. A workflow with no ranked search still needs evidence that the required material was ingested, parsed, and available to the output.


Direct source navigation reduces review friction. In our[source-linked claim charts](https://www.tryandai.com/product/claim-charts) , a reviewer can move from a claim limitation to the underlying patent passage in the same view, then approve, reject, or refine the mapping. The link makes review possible. The reviewer’s source check establishes whether the mapping is sound.


## 5. Test patent-specific edge cases


Clean patents and text-native PDFs can make a tool look more dependable than it is. Include failure modes that reflect the team’s actual technologies, jurisdictions, and matters.


Edge case What it reveals Useful behavior


Long dependent claim Whether inherited limitations disappear Preserves the full dependency chain and addresses each inherited element


Section 112(f) limitation Whether functional similarity is confused with disclosed structure Connects the claimed function to corresponding structure in the specification and applies the construction consistently


Prosecution disclaimer Whether claim meaning survives across the workflow Carries the relevant statement into search, mapping, and analysis


Figure-only disclosure Whether visual evidence is ignored Identifies the figure and feature, keeps its context, and supplies a reviewable pinpoint reference


Poor optical character recognition (OCR) or multi-column NPL Whether extraction corrupts technical content Preserves equations, symbols, tables, and reading order, or flags the passage for manual handling


Non-English family member Whether family and translation context are reliable Links the correct publication, language, family relationship, and translated passage


Priority or public-availability trap Whether legally distinct dates are collapsed Separates priority, filing, publication, archive, sale, and other dates relevant to the theory


Semantic near-match Whether shared nouns are mistaken for disclosure Rejects a passage that lacks the claimed structure, sequence, or relationship


Section 103 combination Whether multi-reference analysis stays coherent Maps each limitation to the correct reference and keeps the combination rationale distinct from cited evidence


Archived product evidence Whether web provenance survives Preserves the web address, capture date, source context, and exact passage or image used


Repeat the hardest items under the same settings and save every output. When behavior changes, ask the vendor to identify the product, model, corpus, parsing, or configuration cause and rerun the failed item after any fix.


## 6. Clear security and confidentiality before protected data


Security is a threshold review. Use public, sanitized, or separately approved material throughout the pilot. Protected live-matter data should enter a rollout only after the required client, contractual, security, export, and matter permissions are in place.


The American Bar Association’s[Formal Opinion 512](https://www.americanbar.org/content/dam/aba/administrative/professional_responsibility/ethics-opinions/aba-formal-opinion-512.pdf) connects generative AI use to duties including competence, confidentiality, communication, supervision, candor, and reasonable fees. Its confidentiality analysis makes understanding a tool’s terms, policies, security, and information handling part of the lawyer’s evaluation.


Require written answers and controlling terms for:


- **Data use:** Whether inputs, files, outputs, prompts, metadata, or feedback can train models, improve products, support analytics, or receive human review.
- **Retention and deletion:** What the vendor and its subprocessors retain in active systems, logs, and backups, for how long, and what deletion covers.
- **Subprocessors and location:** Which model and cloud providers process data, where processing occurs, and how changes are communicated.
- **Access and technical controls:** Single sign-on (SSO), multi-factor authentication, role-based access controls (RBAC), matter permissions, ethical walls, audit logs, encryption, vulnerability management, and key management.
- **Incidents and legal process:** Notice timing, investigation duties, evidence preservation, remediation, subpoenas, government demands, and cooperation with client notices.
- **Ownership, exit, and resilience:** Rights in inputs and outputs, usable export, deletion certification, business continuity, disaster recovery, and service commitments.


Patent teams also need export-control and foreign-filing analysis for unpublished technical information. The USPTO guidance identifies risks when AI systems process information abroad or disclose controlled technology to a foreign person. A System and Organization Controls 2 (SOC 2) Type II report can support the controls review. It does not replace use-specific contract terms or matter-level access design.


## 7. Run the complete workflow and observe the users


Accuracy in an isolated browser session is only one part of fit. Production work includes identity, files, matters, templates, review, export, and records.


Run one task through the intended environment. Confirm that the system can:


- Create and restrict a matter under the team’s identity and access model.
- Ingest the native PDFs, scans, spreadsheets, Word files, videos, and prosecution histories the workflow uses without losing important structure.
- Preserve source links and review status when work moves into Word, Excel, a document management system, or a client template.
- Maintain versions, reviewer identity, approvals, and an exportable audit trail.
- Support an application programming interface (API) or bulk process when the use case requires scale.
- Remove access promptly and preserve required records when a user leaves or a matter closes.


Observe completed work rather than relying on satisfaction surveys alone. Include a senior decision-maker, a day-to-day user, and the person who will administer the system. Record abandoned tasks, workarounds, training time, help requests, corrections, and whether users would choose the tool for the next comparable task.


Support is part of the product experience. Submit a substantive analysis issue, an ingestion or export problem, and an administration question through the normal channel. Keep the first response, useful response, resolution, root-cause explanation, and rerun result.


## 8. Compare total cost with review included


Generation time is rarely the whole economic story. Attorney verification and correction determine whether a tool creates capacity or moves work into another queue.


Capture recurring costs such as licenses, usage, administration, support, review labor, overages, and ongoing training. Capture one-time costs such as implementation, security and legal review, integrations, migration, initial training, and exit work. Allocate shared costs consistently across the tools and human baseline.


Then compare like with like:


- Use the same task set, work-product acceptance rule, labor rates, and time horizon.
- Compare the fully loaded cost per accepted output, rather than the cost per generated output.
- Count setup, monitoring, review, correction, and manual completion time.
- Separate the temporary cost of running the pilot from expected production cost.
- Model expected volume and usage-based charges, including a low, expected, and high-use case.
- Identify what saved time will actually enable before assigning it economic value.


The billing model changes the benefit. On a fixed-fee matter, lower delivery cost can improve margin. On an hourly matter, fewer hours may reduce billed revenue while improving turnaround, capacity, or client value. Formal Opinion 512 also explains that hourly billing remains tied to time actually spent and that charges related to AI tools must be reasonable.


## 9. Use a staged pilot


A focused pilot for one workflow can usually fit into several working weeks. A second workflow needs its own inputs and success conditions because drafting, search, charting, and portfolio analysis expose different risks.


Phase Work Evidence produced


Preparation Approve the use case, data class, expected result, reviewers, non-negotiable requirements, and baseline method Written pilot brief and permission for every input


Test-set build Assemble representative items, known answers, failure modes, and human baseline work Frozen input packs and review records


Controlled runs Configure each tool, run equivalent tasks, and preserve every output and setting Product logs, outputs, versions, and raw timing


Substantive review Check citations and required content, repeat edge cases, and resolve reviewer disagreements Findings by source, limitation, task, and failure type


Operational review Test integrations, access, adoption, support, security terms, and total cost End-to-end export, control evidence, user observations, tickets, and cost model


Decision Document decisive strengths, unresolved risks, accepted limits, owners, and next review triggers Go, limited-rollout, or no-go record


Keep the approved input restrictions in place for every phase. Extend a pilot only when more evidence will answer a defined question, such as an underrepresented document type, an unstable repeat run, or a documented product fix worth retesting.


## 10. Make a bounded decision and keep evaluating


Read the findings side by side. A **go** means the tool meets the defined workflow requirements, the team accepts the remaining limitations, and the required data and access controls are in place. A **limited rollout** means the useful workflow can be contained by explicit restrictions while a remediable gap is addressed. A **no-go** means a decisive accuracy, confidentiality, security, workflow, or economic problem remains unresolved.


For a limited rollout, name the permitted workflow, data class, users, required review, blocked features, remediation owner, and reevaluation trigger. “Use with caution” is too vague to govern a matter.


Evaluation continues after procurement. Review accepted work frequently at the start, then move to a regular schedule based on risk and usage. Rerun the test set after a material change to the model, retrieval corpus, parsing, integration, retention policy, subprocessors, or contract. The National Institute of Standards and Technology[AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) organizes this work around governance, mapping, measurement, and management, a useful pattern for keeping an approval current.


## Frequently asked questions


### How many patent AI tools should a team pilot?


Pilot only the finalists the team can review deeply. A small field leaves more attorney time for source-level inspection and repeated edge cases. Remove any option that cannot support the required workflow or data class before the substantive test.


### What if the team has no gold-standard work product?


Create the first accepted answer from public or properly approved material. Have experienced reviewers identify the required issues, acceptable sources, decisive passages, and reasonable range of outcomes, then resolve disagreements before running the tool. For prior art search, preserve known relevant references while allowing reviewers to accept new art.


### Can a general AI assistant serve as the baseline?


Yes, when it can perform the defined task, such as summarizing a supplied document or drafting routine text. Claim-aware search, patent-family context, source-linked mapping, and litigation exports require a purpose-built workflow. The current human process remains the baseline for work a general assistant cannot complete.
